title: How Long Does Alcohol Stay on Your Breath? Breathalyzer Timeline
excerpt: How long alcohol stays on your breath and shows on a breathalyzer, why gum and mouthwash don't help, how long the smell lasts, and when you're safe to drive.
metaDescription: How long alcohol stays on your breath and shows on a breathalyzer, how long the smell lasts, why mouthwash and gum don't help, and the morning-after math.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** alcohol stays on your breath for as long as it's in your blood. Breath alcohol comes from your lungs, not your stomach, so a breathalyzer can pick it up until your body has finished clearing the alcohol. Most people clear about one standard drink per hour, or roughly 0.015% blood alcohol content (BAC) per hour. That means one drink usually leaves your breath within one to two hours, while a heavy night can still show on a breathalyzer 12 hours or more later. The *smell* can hang around a bit longer, and no amount of gum, mints, coffee, or mouthwash speeds any of it up.

> **Safety first:** This article explains how breath alcohol works in general terms. It is not legal advice and it is not a way to decide whether you can drive. Breathalyzer estimates vary from person to person, home devices can be off, and being under the legal limit is not the same as being unimpaired. If you've been drinking and aren't sure, don't drive. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US)** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and the person should not be left to "sleep it off."

## How Alcohol Gets Onto Your Breath

Most people assume alcohol breath comes from the drink sitting in your mouth or stomach. That's only true for the first few minutes. After that, almost all of the alcohol on your breath comes from your lungs.

Here's the path:

1. **You swallow a drink.** Alcohol is absorbed into your bloodstream mostly through your small intestine, with some through the stomach.
2. **Your blood carries it everywhere.** Alcohol dissolves easily in water, so it spreads into nearly every tissue in your body, including the blood flowing through your lungs.
3. **It crosses into the air in your lungs.** Your lungs are built to swap gases between blood and air. Alcohol is volatile, meaning it evaporates easily, so some of it moves out of the blood and into the tiny air sacs (alveoli) deep in your lungs.
4. **You breathe it out.** Every exhale carries a small amount of alcohol vapor. The more alcohol in your blood, the more on your breath.

This is the key fact behind breathalyzers. Because breath alcohol comes from blood, the amount in deep-lung air rises and falls with your blood alcohol. In the US, breath-test devices are calibrated on the assumption that 2,100 milliliters of deep-lung air contains about the same amount of alcohol as 1 milliliter of blood (often written as a 2100:1 ratio). The real ratio varies somewhat between people and even within one person over a night, which is one reason breath and blood tests don't always match exactly.

It also explains why you can't "air out" your breath. As long as there's alcohol in your blood, your lungs keep releasing it.

## How Long Alcohol Stays on Your Breath: The Timeline

Since breath alcohol tracks blood alcohol, the question really becomes: how long until your blood alcohol reaches zero? That depends on two things: how high your BAC climbed, and how fast your body clears it.

### How fast your body clears alcohol

Your liver does most of the work, using an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase to convert alcohol into a compound called acetaldehyde, then into acetate, which your body breaks down further. A small share of alcohol leaves unchanged through your breath, sweat, and urine.

Unlike most drugs, alcohol is cleared at a fairly steady rate once your BAC is above a low level, because the liver's enzymes are working at full capacity. For most adults, that rate lands somewhere around **0.015% BAC per hour**, though research has found a range of roughly 0.010% to 0.025% per hour depending on the person. Regular heavy drinkers sometimes clear alcohol faster; occasional drinkers often sit nearer the middle.

### The rough math

Divide your peak BAC by 0.015 and you get a rough number of hours until you're near zero.

| Peak BAC | Roughly how you got there* | Approximate time to clear (at 0.015%/hr) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.02% | One drink | About 1 to 2 hours |
| 0.05% | Two to three drinks | About 3 to 4 hours |
| 0.08% | Three to five drinks | About 5 to 6 hours |
| 0.12% | Five to seven drinks | About 8 hours |
| 0.15% | Six to nine drinks | About 10 hours |
| 0.20% | A very heavy night | About 13 hours or more |

*The number of drinks needed to reach a given BAC varies widely with body weight, sex, food, and how fast you drank. These ranges are illustrations, not predictions for you.

Two practical takeaways from this table:

- **The clock starts at your peak, not your last drink.** BAC usually keeps climbing for 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink as the alcohol finishes absorbing. If you stop drinking at midnight, you may not peak until 1 a.m.
- **Morning-after readings are common.** If you drank heavily until 2 a.m. and slept six hours, the math says you may still have alcohol in your blood when you wake up. Many people who feel "fine" the next morning would still register on a breathalyzer, and some would be over a legal driving limit.

For a fuller look at how long alcohol lingers in blood, urine, saliva, and hair, see our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system).

## How Long Does Alcohol Show on a Breathalyzer?

This is the same question with a different tool, so the answer is the same: a breathalyzer shows alcohol for as long as there is alcohol in your blood. A breathalyzer can't tell what you drank last night. It measures what's coming out of your lungs right now.

Some details that matter:

- **Low levels may not register on every device.** Many consumer breathalyzers can't reliably detect very low concentrations, so the tail end of the curve may read as zero on one device and as a trace on a more sensitive one.
- **Police devices are more precise.** Evidential breath-test instruments used at police stations are more accurate than roadside screening devices and far more accurate than most cheap home models.
- **Ignition interlock devices often use a low threshold.** Interlocks installed in some drivers' cars are typically set to fail at a fairly low breath alcohol level, so a morning-after reading that you'd expect to be "nearly zero" can still lock the car.

### Legal limits for reference

In the US, the general limit for drivers 21 and older is 0.08% BAC in every state except Utah, which uses 0.05%. Commercial drivers are held to 0.04%, and drivers under 21 face "zero tolerance" limits, usually 0.00% to 0.02% depending on the state. Many other countries use 0.05% or lower. These are legal lines, not safety lines. Reaction time and judgment start to slip well below them.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Pass a Breathalyzer?

People ask this question for very different reasons, from a workplace test to an ignition interlock to simply wanting to drive home safely. The honest answer is that no online calculator can tell you, because it depends on:

- **How much you drank and how strong it was.** A "drink" can range from a light beer to a double pour of a high-proof spirit. If you're not sure how much alcohol was in what you had, standard drink sizes are a useful starting point: 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, or 1.5 oz of 40% (80-proof) spirits each contain about the same amount of alcohol.
- **How fast you drank it.** Three drinks in an hour push your BAC much higher than three drinks over an evening.
- **Your body size and composition.** Alcohol spreads through body water. Smaller people, and people with more body fat relative to body water, tend to reach higher BACs from the same amount.
- **Sex.** On average, women reach higher BACs than men from the same amount of alcohol, mostly because of differences in body water.
- **Food.** Eating before or while drinking slows absorption and lowers your peak, though it doesn't change how fast you clear alcohol once it's in your blood.
- **Your personal clearance rate.** This is the part nobody can see from the outside.

A cautious rule of thumb: estimate your peak BAC, divide by 0.015, then add a buffer. If the answer is close, assume you'd still fail and don't drive. Personal breathalyzers can be a useful extra check, but cheap ones can be badly off, so don't treat a single home reading as permission.

## How Long Does Alcohol Smell Last?

The smell and the breathalyzer reading are related but not identical.

Pure ethanol, the alcohol in drinks, has only a faint smell. Most of what people recognize as "alcohol breath" comes from:

- **The drink itself, for the first few minutes.** Beer, wine, and dark spirits carry flavor compounds called congeners (the substances besides ethanol that give drinks their flavor and color). These are strongest right after drinking.
- **By-products of breaking alcohol down.** As your liver processes alcohol, some of the resulting compounds are also exhaled and sweated out. They give the stale, slightly sweet "morning-after" smell.
- **A dry mouth.** Alcohol reduces saliva, and a dry mouth lets odor-causing bacteria thrive. That's why morning breath after drinking can be especially bad even once most of the alcohol is gone.

In practice, the smell usually tracks the breathalyzer curve and fades as your BAC drops, but the bad-breath part can outlast it by a few hours if you're dehydrated and haven't brushed. After a very heavy night, people often notice the smell on their breath and skin well into the next day.

### Can someone smell alcohol on you if a breathalyzer reads zero?

Sometimes. If you've cleared the alcohol but still have a dry mouth and residue on your teeth and tongue, a stale smell can linger. Brushing, scraping your tongue, drinking water, and eating usually take care of it. The opposite is also true: someone can have a meaningful BAC while smelling of very little, especially after drinking clear spirits like vodka. Smell is a poor guide to how much alcohol someone has in their blood.

## Does Mouthwash Affect a Breathalyzer?

It can, briefly. Many mouthwashes contain a significant amount of alcohol. Original Listerine, for example, is around 27% alcohol, more than most wines. Rinsing with it leaves alcohol on the surfaces of your mouth, and a breathalyzer taken right after can show a falsely high reading.

That mouth alcohol fades quickly, usually within about 15 minutes, because it evaporates and gets diluted by saliva. This is the reason police and testing programs use a waiting period, typically 15 to 20 minutes of observation during which the person doesn't eat, drink, smoke, or put anything in their mouth, before an official breath test.

The same short-lived effect can come from:

- **A drink you just finished** (residual alcohol in the mouth)
- **Burping, vomiting, or acid reflux**, which can bring alcohol from the stomach back up into the mouth
- **Some breath sprays, cough syrups, and fermented foods or drinks**, if they contain alcohol

Two things mouthwash cannot do: it can't hide alcohol that's really in your blood, and it can't lower your reading. It can only add a temporary false bump on top.

## Myths About Getting Rid of Alcohol Breath

Because breath alcohol comes from your lungs, nearly every popular trick only affects your mouth. Here's how the common ones stack up.

| Trick | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| Gum or mints | Masks the smell in your mouth for a few minutes. No effect on breath alcohol or BAC. |
| Coffee | May make you feel more alert, but doesn't lower BAC. An alert drunk person is still impaired. |
| Brushing your teeth | Helps the smell from your mouth. Doesn't change what comes from your lungs. |
| Drinking lots of water | Helps with dry mouth and dehydration. Doesn't meaningfully speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. |
| A cold shower | Wakes you up. No effect on BAC. |
| Exercise or sweating it out | Only a tiny fraction of alcohol leaves through sweat and breath; the liver does the real work. |
| Eating a big meal after drinking | Food in your stomach slows absorption of alcohol you *haven't absorbed yet*, but doesn't remove alcohol already in your blood. |
| Holding your breath, hyperventilating, or pennies in your mouth | Can nudge a reading up or down slightly by changing breath temperature or volume, but they're unreliable and don't change your actual BAC. The penny trick has no effect. |

We go through the real limits of each of these in our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism). The short version is that time is the only thing that reliably lowers your BAC.

## What Can Cause a False Positive on a Breathalyzer?

Breathalyzers are generally accurate when used properly, but a few situations can produce readings that don't reflect your blood alcohol:

- **Mouth alcohol** from recent drinking, mouthwash, reflux, or vomiting, as described above.
- **Device type.** Many cheap home breathalyzers use a semiconductor sensor, which can react to substances other than ethanol. Fuel-cell sensors, used in most police screening devices and better home models, are more specific to alcohol.
- **Calibration.** Breathalyzers drift over time and need periodic recalibration. An uncalibrated home device can be off in either direction.
- **Some medical conditions.** People with poorly controlled diabetes, or who are following very low-carbohydrate diets, can produce compounds called ketones that some less specific devices may misread. Evidential police instruments are designed to account for this.
- **Breathing pattern.** Breath temperature and how deeply you exhale affect readings, which is why devices ask for a long, steady breath.

If you're ever disputing an official result, that's a question for a lawyer, not a blog post. For everyday use, the practical lesson is simpler: if a home device reads even a little above zero and you're about to drive, don't.

## Breath Alcohol vs. Other Tests

Breath tests are one of several ways to measure alcohol, and each covers a different window:

- **Breath:** shows alcohol currently in your blood. Window ends when your BAC reaches zero, typically within a day.
- **Blood:** the most direct measure of current alcohol. Same basic window as breath.
- **Saliva:** similar to breath, roughly up to a day.
- **Urine (standard test):** similar to blood for alcohol itself. Some tests instead look for alcohol by-products such as ethyl glucuronide (EtG), which can be detectable for days after heavy drinking.
- **Hair:** can show patterns of drinking over months, not single nights.

So if you're worried about a workplace or monitoring program that uses a urine test, the breath timeline doesn't apply. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in urine](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-urine) covers those tests.

## Is It Safe to Drive the Morning After?

This is the real question behind a lot of "how long does alcohol stay on your breath" searches, so it's worth being direct.

- **You can still be over the limit in the morning.** Sleep doesn't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. If you drank heavily late into the night, there's a realistic chance you'll still have alcohol in your blood at breakfast.
- **Feeling OK isn't a reliable test.** People are poor judges of their own BAC, especially as it falls. You may feel normal while still being impaired.
- **A hangover is impairment too.** Even after your BAC hits zero, a bad hangover can slow your reactions and attention. Research on next-day effects has found that hangover can affect driving-related skills, even with no alcohol left in the blood.

If you'll need to drive in the morning, the most reliable plan is to stop drinking early enough, drink less, or arrange another way home and to work. Our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) covers the recovery side.

## When to Worry: Signs It's More Than a Hangover

For most social drinkers, alcohol breath the morning after is just a sign the night was bigger than planned. But a few situations call for help, not a breath mint.

**Call 911 (US) or your local emergency number if someone who has been drinking:**

- Is confused, can't be woken, or keeps passing out
- Is vomiting while drowsy or unresponsive
- Has slow breathing (fewer than about eight breaths a minute) or long gaps between breaths
- Has a seizure
- Has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin, or a low body temperature

These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't leave the person alone, don't let them "sleep it off," and turn them on their side if they're lying down so they won't choke if they vomit.

**See a doctor if:**

- You regularly smell alcohol on your breath or a sweet, fruity smell even when you haven't been drinking much. A fruity breath smell can be a sign of a blood sugar problem called ketoacidosis, which needs medical care.
- You find you need a drink in the morning to stop shaking, sweating, or anxiety. Those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous and is worth discussing with a doctor plainly and without embarrassment.
- You have ongoing bad breath that doesn't improve with brushing and hydration. That's usually a dental or gum issue rather than alcohol.

## How to Make Alcohol Breath Less of a Problem

Since you can't speed up your liver, the useful moves are about lowering how high your BAC goes and taking care of the mouth part of the smell:

1. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows absorption and lowers your peak BAC, which shortens the whole curve.
2. **Pace yourself.** One standard drink per hour or slower keeps your BAC from stacking up.
3. **Alternate with water.** It won't flush alcohol out, but it helps with dry mouth, which is a big part of next-day bad breath.
4. **Know what you're drinking.** A craft IPA or a heavy pour can contain far more alcohol than a "standard drink," which throws off any timing estimate.
5. **Stop earlier if you need to be sober in the morning.** Count backward from when you need to be at zero, using the 0.015%-per-hour rule with a generous buffer.
6. **Brush, floss, and scrape your tongue before bed and in the morning.** It handles the mouth half of the smell.

For more on the habits that do the most for the morning after, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's popular as a hangover supplement. It's worth being clear about what it can and can't do in the context of breath alcohol.

- **What the research suggests:** animal and lab studies indicate DHM may affect how the body handles alcohol and its by-products, and may reduce some of alcohol's effects on the brain. Human data are limited, and most of what exists looks at how people feel the next day rather than at blood alcohol.
- **What it doesn't do:** there is no good evidence that DHM lowers your breath or blood alcohol in any meaningful way, and it should never factor into whether you drive. It also won't stop a breathalyzer from detecting alcohol.

If you want to try DHM for how you feel the morning after, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which pairs DHM with L-cysteine, and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts. Think of it as a possible comfort aid, not a sobriety tool.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol on your breath comes from your lungs, which release alcohol from your blood. It stays on your breath as long as it's in your blood.
- Most people clear about 0.015% BAC per hour. One drink usually clears in one to two hours; a heavy night can still show on a breathalyzer 12 hours or more later.
- The smell can linger a little past the alcohol itself because of by-products and dry mouth, but it fades along with your BAC.
- Mouthwash, burping, and recent drinks can cause a short-lived false high reading, which is why official tests use a 15-to-20-minute waiting period.
- Gum, mints, coffee, water, showers, and exercise don't lower your BAC. Only time does.
- If you're unsure whether you're sober enough to drive, you aren't. Make another plan.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How long does alcohol stay on your breath?**

Alcohol stays on your breath, and shows on a breathalyzer, for as long as there is alcohol in your blood. Your body clears roughly 0.015% BAC per hour on average, so one drink usually clears in one to two hours, while a heavy night can leave measurable breath alcohol 12 hours or more later. The smell can linger a little longer than that, because the by-products of breaking alcohol down also leave through your lungs.

**How long after drinking can you pass a breathalyzer?**

There is no single number, because it depends on how high your blood alcohol got and how fast your body clears it. A rough guide is to divide your peak BAC by 0.015 to get the hours until you're near zero: a peak of 0.08% takes about five to six hours, and a peak of 0.15% takes about ten. Individual rates vary, so treat any estimate as a minimum, and don't drive if you're unsure. Being under the legal limit is not the same as being unimpaired.

**Does mouthwash make you fail a breathalyzer?**

It can for a short time. Many mouthwashes contain alcohol (original Listerine is around 27%), and rinsing leaves alcohol in your mouth that can produce a high reading right away. That mouth alcohol fades within roughly 15 minutes, which is why police are trained to observe a person for about 15 to 20 minutes before an official breath test. Mouthwash will not lower a real reading; it only adds a temporary false one.

**Can gum, mints, or coffee get rid of alcohol breath?**

No. They can cover the smell in your mouth for a few minutes, but the alcohol on your breath comes from your lungs, where alcohol in your blood passes into the air you exhale. Nothing you put in your mouth changes that. Only time lowers your blood alcohol, and the breath alcohol and smell drop along with it.

**Why do I still smell like alcohol the next day?**

If you drank heavily, there may still be alcohol in your blood the next morning, and it leaves through your lungs and skin. Your body also produces by-products while breaking alcohol down, and some of those have a stale, sweetish smell of their own. Brushing your teeth helps the mouth part, and a shower helps the sweat part, but the breath smell fades only as your body finishes processing the alcohol.

**Can a breathalyzer detect alcohol from the night before?**

Yes, if there is still alcohol in your blood. After a heavy night that ends in the early hours, many people still have a measurable blood alcohol level the next morning, and some are still over a legal driving limit. A breathalyzer measures what is in your breath now, not what you drank, so the morning-after reading reflects how much alcohol your body hasn't cleared yet.

**Do breathalyzers measure alcohol in your mouth or your lungs?**

They're designed to measure alcohol from deep in your lungs, which tracks the alcohol in your blood. Recent drinking, burping, vomiting, or reflux can leave alcohol in the mouth that briefly pushes a reading up, which is why official testing includes a waiting period and devices ask for a long, steady breath.

**Does DHM lower your breathalyzer reading?**

There is no good evidence that DHM lowers breath or blood alcohol in people in any meaningful way, and it should never be used to decide whether you can drive. Some animal research suggests DHM may affect how alcohol is processed, but that hasn't been shown to change breathalyzer results in humans. Only time brings your BAC down.
